analysis.one_liner: Taxes coal, oil, and natural gas at $10 per ton of carbon, rising annually.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have placed an excise tax on coal, petroleum, and natural gas, set at $10 per ton of the carbon the fuel contains. The tax would rise by another $10 every year until U.S. carbon dioxide emissions fell to 20 percent of their 1990 level, at which point the rate would freeze. Fossil fuel producers and importers would pay the tax, and its cost would show up in higher prices for gasoline, heating, and electricity. The bill itself imposed the tax but did not enact any rebate; it stated only that the revenue could be used to cut taxes for low- and middle-income families or fund clean energy research.
analysis.who_benefits: In the long run, everyone exposed to climate damage, since the escalating tax is designed to push carbon dioxide emissions down to 20 percent of their 1990 level. If Congress had later directed the revenue as the bill's findings suggest, low- and middle-income taxpayers would also have gained from tax cuts or clean-energy funding — but the bill text does not enact that; it leaves the revenue decision to future law.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's stated purpose is to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by making carbon-intensive fuels more expensive to burn, citing IPCC findings that emissions must fall dramatically to avoid major climate impacts.

The tax starts at $10 per ton of carbon content and increases by $10 each year until U.S. emissions fall to 20 percent of their 1990 level, after which the rate freezes — a built-in escalator tied to a concrete emissions target.

The bill's findings state that revenue from the tax could be used to decrease taxes on low- and middle-income taxpayers or to fund research into alternative green energy sources, though the bill text does not itself enact any of those uses.

Exports and fuel for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve are exempt, and refunds are provided where carbon is embedded in non-fuel products, limiting the tax to fuels actually burned in the United States.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and importers pay the tax directly on coal, petroleum, and natural gas, and they pass the cost through to households and businesses in higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity. Because the bill does not include a rebate, the burden would land on energy consumers, and energy costs take a larger bite out of low-income household budgets.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes the tax without enacting any rebate or dividend. Its findings say revenue could offset taxes on low- and middle-income families, but nothing in the bill text requires it, so the initial cost would fall directly on consumers through higher energy prices.

A carbon tax is inherently regressive in its early years: lower-income households spend a larger share of their budget on gasoline, heating, and electricity, so they would feel the price increase first and hardest unless Congress separately legislated offsets.

A unilateral U.S. carbon tax raises prices for American energy-intensive producers relative to foreign competitors, and the bill's response — exempting exports — does not shield domestic industries competing against imports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The climate logic is sound: pricing carbon per ton, with a rate that keeps rising until emissions hit the target, directly attacks the problem the findings describe. But the bill as written is a tax first and a rebate never — it passes the cost to households at the pump and on the utility bill without enacting the low- and middle-income relief its own findings point to. An honest supporter would have paired the tax with an upfront dividend; an honest critic concedes that climate inaction carries its own large costs. It died without any of this ever being debated on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Pete Stark introduced the bill on April 26, 2007, with Jim McDermott as an original cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day.
Three Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The action history shows no further action after the committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and importers, who avoided a rising tax on every ton of carbon in coal, oil, and gas they sold; households also avoided near-term energy price increases, at the cost of leaving the emissions problem unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers avoided the carbon tax

for.name: Rep. Pete Stark
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Rep. Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Joined Stark in introducing the bill as an original cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill never reached a vote, so no party split was ever recorded on it.

industries.industry: Coal producers and coal-fired electric utilities
industries.note: Coal has the highest carbon content per unit of energy of the taxable fuels, so it would bear the heaviest burden under the per-ton tax, and the escalating rate would grow every year. Coal's interest in blocking the bill ran against the bill's goal of cutting the emissions coal produces most.

industries.industry: Oil and petroleum product producers and importers
industries.note: Every ton of carbon in petroleum and petroleum products sold in the U.S. would be taxed at $10 and rising, directly raising the cost of gasoline and heating oil for their customers.
Natural gas is explicitly included as a taxable fuel, though its lower carbon content means a smaller per-unit tax than coal.
